summary: Provides up-to-date recommendations for the secure use of TLS and DTLS, which protect data for many application protocols. It responds to attacks seen over the years on common cipher suites and modes of operation. It obsoletes RFC 7525. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9325 gives updated rules for configuring TLS and DTLS. It rejects older versions, favors TLS 1.3, and keeps TLS 1.2 support for compatibility.

questions: what are the best practices for tls and dtls
which tls 1.2 cipher suites are recommended
subtitle: A best-practice guide to protocol versions, authentication, cipher choices, and key handling for TLS and DTLS.

tldr.problem: Attacks and changes in deployment have made older guidance for TLS and DTLS insufficient for many services.
tldr.mechanism: The Best Current Practice sets requirements for supported versions, strict TLS, session resumption, negotiation, cipher suites, public keys, and certificate revocation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9325 obsoletes RFC 7525, recommends TLS 1.3, and still requires support for TLS 1.2. It has been updated by RFC 9852 and RFC 10015.

today: RFC 9325 is Best Current Practice 195 and obsoletes RFC 7525. It updates RFC 5288 and RFC 6066, and has been updated by RFC 9852 and RFC 10015.

sections.title: Scope of the Recommendations
sections.content:
RFC 9325 gives guidance for services and software that use TLS or DTLS to protect application protocols. It applies to both unless a recommendation is marked for only one protocol. Secure transport protocols that reuse the TLS handshake, such as QUIC, are not directly in scope.

The document replaces RFC 7525 because TLS 1.3 became widely available after that earlier guidance was written. It encourages migration from most uses of TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3, while treating its recommendations as a minimum baseline that may need to be strengthened for a particular service.

The RFC describes this Best Current Practice as a point-in-time statement. It does not make recommendations for post-quantum cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: This document updates security guidance for applications that use TLS or DTLS. It is a baseline for common cases, and later changes in attacks or technology may require new guidance.

sections.title: Protocol Versions to Negotiate
sections.content:
Implementations must not negotiate SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0, or TLS 1.1. They must support TLS 1.2 because it remains important for interoperability and can be used securely when the document's recommendations are followed.

Implementations should support TLS 1.3 and must prefer it over earlier TLS versions when available. A new transport protocol that incorporates the TLS or DTLS handshake or record layer must use version 1.3 only. New application protocols that use TLS or DTLS for encryption must support versions 1.2 and 1.3, except where broad interoperability is not a concern.

For DTLS, implementations must not negotiate version 1.0, must support version 1.2, and should support and prefer version 1.3.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not negotiate the older SSL or TLS versions listed in the RFC. Prefer TLS 1.3 when both sides support it, while keeping TLS 1.2 available for compatibility.

sections.title: Strict TLS, Compression, and Session Resumption
sections.content:
When a protocol offers both a TLS-only port and an upgrade from plaintext, implementations must support the TLS-only method and administrators must prefer it. If only an upgrade method exists, implementations must offer a policy that forbids plaintext and administrators must use that policy. TLS 1.2 implementations should not support TLS-level compression.

Session-resumption information must be authenticated and encrypted. Ticket-encryption keys must be changed regularly and old keys destroyed when their validity ends; ticket validity must also be limited. For TLS 1.3 resumption, servers should use a key exchange that restores forward secrecy.

TLS 1.2 implementations must support the renegotiation and extended-master-secret protections described in the RFC. Renegotiation is not part of TLS 1.3.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with a protected connection instead of relying on a later upgrade from plaintext. Protect and rotate session-ticket keys, and use the protocol's safeguards when resuming or renegotiating a session.

sections.title: Names, Application Protocols, and Early Data
sections.content:
TLS implementations must support Server Name Indication when the higher-level protocol benefits from it. A server that does not recognize the presented name should fail the handshake, and a client should abort if the server presents a certificate for a different name.

Implementations must support Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN). Servers should reject a connection when they support none of the client's offered protocols, and clients should abort if the server selects no offered protocol. Services sharing a name or providing the same service should maintain equivalent security levels.

Applications must avoid TLS 1.3 zero-round-trip-time data unless a specification for that application protocol explains when it is appropriate and secure.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server must agree on the intended name and application protocol. Do not use TLS early data unless the application protocol has rules that make its use safe.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Public-Key Strength
sections.content:
Implementations must not negotiate cipher suites with no encryption, RC4, or less than the stated minimum security level. They should avoid suites with weaker-than-recommended strength, static RSA key transport, and non-ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key agreement. They must support and prefer forward-secret suites.

For TLS 1.2, the RFC recommends four ECDHE-based AES-GCM suites using RSA or ECDSA authentication. Clients should offer the RSA/AES-128-GCM suite first, and servers must prefer it over weaker suites when it is offered. CBC suites should not be used unless encrypt-then-MAC is negotiated.

DHE keys must be at least 2048 bits, ECDH curves smaller than 224 bits must not be used, and RSA server certificates must have a modulus of at least 2048 bits. The RFC recommends SHA-256 and prohibits SHA-1 and MD5 for the covered use.
sections.plainLanguage: Use cipher suites that provide strong encryption and forward secrecy. The RFC sets minimum sizes for Diffie-Hellman, elliptic-curve, and RSA keys.

sections.title: Validate Hosts, Keys, and Certificates
sections.content:
Host-name validation is essential: a valid certificate alone does not prove that the connection reached the intended server. A name learned through an insecure cleartext DNS lookup should not be used as the reference name.

TLS 1.2 implementations are recommended to derive the explicit part of an AES-GCM nonce from the record sequence number. Implementations should avoid reusing Diffie-Hellman exponents in ways that defeat forward secrecy, and servers reusing elliptic-curve keys should use a safe curve or validate received points.

Implementations must have a strategy for distrusting revoked certificates. Servers should support OCSP and OCSP stapling, though the RFC notes that certificate revocation still has no complete and efficient solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Check that a certificate belongs to the server name the client intended to reach. Protect old sessions from later key theft and use a process for rejecting revoked certificates.
